text: If this program's SOC course covered alert fatigue, it covered it from the analyst's side, where a flood of alerts arrives and the person on the other end starts tuning it all out. This lesson covers the same problem from where it actually starts: the configuration side. Alert fatigue isn't something that just happens to a team — it's something a deployment creates for itself, on day one, the moment thresholds get set more sensitively than the environment can support.

It feels responsible to set a CPU alert at 70% instead of 85%, on the theory that catching problems earlier is always better. In practice it backfires. A web server doing completely normal work might sit at 70-75% CPU for stretches every single day — nothing is wrong, but the alert fires anyway, repeatedly. After the third or fourth page for a non-problem, the response stops being investigate and starts being dismiss, and that habit spreads to the alerts that actually matter too.

Set before observing real behavior, a 70% threshold fires ten or more times in the first week alone, pure noise. Set after watching two weeks of this environment's real traffic, the 85% threshold from Lesson 14 never fires on normal load at all — because that's exactly the level chosen to separate normal from actually wrong, instead of a number picked out of thin air before the environment had even taken real traffic.

The fix is starting with the small, high-confidence set from Lesson 14 — sustained high CPU, low disk, failed health checks, failed logins — and genuinely watching how it behaves against real traffic before adding anything else. Only once that set proves itself does it make sense to add a new alert, one at a time, each one earning its place the same way the first four did. Expanding the set is a decision made from observed behavior, not a one-time setup checklist.

Tuned correctly from real behavior instead of guessed at on day one, an alert set stays trustworthy instead of becoming background noise. Next up: a practical five-point checklist that closes out this chapter and confirms monitoring on this environment is actually complete.
